--- title: "Explorando o tidyverse" description: | Primeiro Workshop para o projeto data viz author: "Ana Li" date: "01/12/2025" title-block-banner: "#B8573E" toc: true toc-location: left toc-depth: 3 categories: - tidyverse - Eukaryota - Plantae - R image: work1.png freeze: true --- ::: {.cell} ::: :::{.author-card} :::{.author-card-text} #### Author [Ana li](https://github.com/lesuff/1-Workshop-Explorando-o-Tidyverse) #### Date March 2021 ::: :::{.author-card-image} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-labs/main/images/people/martin.jpg){width=120px style="clip-path: circle();"} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Library Tidyverse Encontre o material [aqui](https://github.com/lesuff/1-Workshop-Explorando-o-Tidyverse); but in practice there are only a few that we use routinely. Our default at ALA labs is to use `viridis` for continuous scales, because it's color-blind friendly, perceptually uniform, and pretty. The default purple-green-yellow color scheme is lovely, but I'm a big fan of 'magma', which has a black-purple-orange-yellow scheme ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(galah) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) library(viridis) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Get field code for states/territories search_fields("state") # layer: cl22 OR stateProvince ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 15 × 3 id description type 1 cl22 Australian States and Territories fields 2 cl927 States including coastal waters fields 3 cl938 Fruit Fly Exclusion Zone - Tri State fields 4 cl2013 ASGS Australian States and Territories fields 5 cl10900 Australia's Indigenous forest estate (2013) v2.0 fields 6 cl10922 PSMA State Electoral Boundaries (2018) fields 7 cl10925 PSMA States (2016) fields 8 cl11174 States and Territories 2021 fields 9 cl11175 State Electoral Divisions 2022 fields 10 cl110922 PSMA State Electoral Boundary Classes (2018) fields 11 cl110925 PSMA States - Abbreviated (2016) fields 12 stateInvasive fields 13 stateProvince State/Territory fields 14 raw_stateProvince State/Territory (unprocessed) fields 15 stateConservation State conservation fields ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Download record counts by state/territory records <- galah_call() %>% galah_group_by(cl22) %>% atlas_counts() # Add state information back to data frame records$State <- factor(seq_len(nrow(records)), labels = records$cl22) # Plot ggplot(records, aes(x = State, y = log10(count), fill = count)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + coord_flip() + scale_fill_viridis(option = "magma", begin = 0.10, end = 0.95) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: My default for categorical color schemes is the 'dark2' palette from `RColorBrewer`; but given the subject matter of our work, it's worth mentioning the wonderful `feather` package by [Shandiya Balasubramaniam](about/Balasubramaniam_Shandiya/index.html), which gives colors based on Australian bird plumage. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # remotes::install_github(repo = "shandiya/feathers") ``` ::: All of this is fine, but what if you have a specific image that you want to take colors from? A logical choice is to pick the colors you want using an image editting program, but if we want to try something automated, there are options in R as well. # Extracting colors [National Eucalypt Day](https://www.eucalyptaustralia.org.au/national-eucalypt-day/national-eucalypt-day/) aims to raise awareness about Eucalypts and celebrate their influence on the lives of Australians. In honour of National Eucalypt day, we wanted to created a plot based on occurrences data held in the Atlas of Living Australia, themed using colours from actual Eucalypts. We used this image from a tweet by Dean Nicolle: ::: {.cell} ::: ![Image of Eucalyptus salubris by Dean Nicolle](./data/Dean_Nicolle_Esalubris_image_small.jpeg) First, get observations of the Eucalypt of the Year 2021 from ALA using the [galah](https://atlasoflivingaustralia.github.io/galah/index.html) package. Specifically, we use `atlas_counts()` to determine how many records of *Eucalyptus salubris* are held by the ALA: ::: {.cell} ::: Here is what the data look like: ::: {.cell} ::: Then get a color scheme from images of the species in question using the [paletter](https://github.com/AndreaCirilloAC/paletter) package (which needs to be installed from GitHub)
::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Note that we downsized the image before running the `paletter` code, as large images take much longer to process. # Creating a plot Once we have this palette, the obvious question is what kind of plot to draw. We could have done a map, but those can be a bit boring. We decided to try something that represented the number of observations we had of this species at ALA, and included color, but was otherwise just a pretty picture that didn't need to contain any further information. Rather than have a traditional x and y axis, therefore, we decided to try out the [igraph](https://igraph.org/r/) package to plot the points in an interesting way. First, we create a vector containing as many points as we want to display, and distribute our colors among them as evenly as possible ::: {.cell} ::: Then we can create a network using `igraph`, and use it to create a layout for our points ::: {.cell} ::: Finally, we draw the plot with [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), removing axes with `theme_void()` ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: That's it! While I like the effect here, I think the `paletter` package is best suited to cases where there are large areas of strongly contrasting colors; it's less ideal for images with subtle color differences. It also doesn't appear to have been updated lately, which may mean it's not being supported any more. But I'm happy with this plot, and would definitely consider using it again.
